Exoplanet Analytics

1. How discoveries accumulated

The file lists 6,445 confirmed planets discovered from 1992 to 2026. Transit accounts for 74% of them, and 2016 was the busiest year with 1,504 discoveries.

2. Planet size against orbit

6,045 planets have both an orbital period and a radius. The dashed box marks the region used in the next section.

3. Is there a gap in the sizes of small planets?

Among 3,495 planets with orbital periods under 100 days and radii between 1 and 4 Earth radii, no clear gap was found: the density has fewer than two distinct peaks.

Robustness check: the same search on the 1,529 of those planets whose stated radius uncertainty is at most 10% of the radius. No clear gap here either: the dip is shallow (valley at 90.2% of the lower peak, above the 90% cutoff).

For context, Fulton et al. (2017) reported a dip in this size range using precise California-Kepler Survey radii. The composite table mixes measurement quality, so a blurrier dip here would not be surprising.

4. How much of a planet's size can its orbit and star explain?

Using orbital period and four host star properties, gradient boosting predicted planet radius on 5-fold cross-validation grouped by host star (6,045 planets in 4,487 systems) with R squared 0.52, against 0.30 for a linear baseline. A typical prediction is off by a factor of about 1.89. Shuffling orbital period hurt the model most.

Method and limits

  • Pipeline. The CSV export is validated and cleaned, stored in DuckDB, and the trend counts come from SQL. Planets with non-positive physical values have those values set to missing.
  • Gap detection. A kernel density estimate of log radius is searched for two prominent peaks. A dip counts only if it falls to 90% of the lower peak or less. Resampling planets gives the interval.
  • Model. Gradient boosting is compared with a ridge regression and with predicting the average. Folds are grouped by host star so planets from one system never appear on both sides of a split.
  • Selection effects. Which planets exist in the table depends on what each method can detect. Transit surveys find close-in planets with measurable radii, and radial velocity mostly gives masses. The patterns here describe the detected population, not all planets.
  • Data quality. The composite table mixes measurements of different precision, and the model and trend analyses ignore the stated uncertainties. The gap search is repeated on precisely measured planets as a check.
  • Interpretation. The model shows association, not cause.
